To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) the prevalence of undiagnosed diabetes in a primary care population is 3%, (ii) the prevalence of ‘high-risk’ of diabetes is 18% and (iii) the two recommended tests to identify ‘high-risk’ individuals are equally effective but identify different people.

(i) the Leicester Risk Assessment score and the Cambridge Risk Score perform similarly, but the Cambridge score is more sensitive; (ii) the Leicester Risk score and HbA 1c identify similar populations, but the Cambridge Risk score identifies different people; and (iii) a high risk score is more likely to be associated with a high risk of diabetes by either HbA  1c or fasting blood glucose.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the practical implications of using HbA1C or fasting glucose as the initial screening test.
the practical implications of the NICE guidance.
the practical implications of choice of screening test in the prevention of Type 2 Diabetes.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
both tests perform similarly, but the Cambridge Risk Assessment is more sensitive and less accurate.

the choice of test to identify people at risk of progression to Type 1 diabetes is not critical, as both HbA1C and fasting glucose will identify similar people, but if one is to use the Leicester Risk Assessment as a first stage screen, then HbA1 is the better choice.
both HbA1 and fasting glucose are equally effective in detecting undiagnosed diabetes and those at high risk for progression of Type 2.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
, in our cohort, the Leicester Risk Assessment would identify more people with Type 2 diabetes, but the Cambridge Risk Assessment would identify a greater number of people at high risk.
both the Leicester Risk Assessment [5] and the Cambridge risk assessment [6] perform well for the identification of high risk of Type 2 Diabetes.

the Leicester Risk Assessment identifies a greater proportion of those at high risk than the Cambridge Risk Assessment, but the Cambridge Risk Assessment identifies more people with undiagnosable diabetes.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the choice of test for initial risk assessment will have a large impact on the number of people identified as ‘high risk’ and therefore the number requiring blood testing.
the choice of test will have a large impact on the proportion of those screened who will be classified as at high risk, and that this will have implications for the cost of screening.

, in the absence of data from randomized controlled trials, the choice of initial test will have a major impact on the number of people who will be identified and the proportion with undiagnoses Type 2 diabetes or at high biochemical risk of developing Type diabetes.
